commentBody: Tough but fair

THAT was a great puzzle. Saturday hardness but a fun puzzle anyway. I love when I can get nothing in a whole section on first pass (NW) and then come back after conquering the rest to watch it all fall in place. “Jazz aficionado” and “flame proof” my favorite clues ;)
I struggled a lot more than I have in quite a while, but in a good way. More Fridays like this, please (heck, more *Saturdays* like this!).

I liked the cluing in this sticky Friday workout.  Lightning conductor, They might raise your kids, and Setting for an uphill climb, were among my favorites.  I was saved by remembering my Faust and Whitman, and by knowing RONALDINHO and HAROLDRAMIS.  I’m not one who objects to trivia heavy puzzles, but I could see this one irking those whose minds are less cluttered with trivial pop culture knowledge than mine.

That was an excellent tough Saturday puzzle for me. Nowhere near a Friday.

I appreciate the difficulty, but I'm really tired of the editors' messing with us.

What I don’t think many folks will say about the puzzle today: ITSABREEZE What I hope to be able to say about Fridays based on this puzzle: WEARESOBACK Actually I can’t say this puzzle took me very long at all—but it felt hard. I had to jump around all over the place, appreciated a lot of tricky clues, was misled several times, learned a lot, and just barely avoided a few Naticks. If this is the level of Fridays going forward I won’t complain. Let’s see…I knew PELE was a soccer god, but a real god too? (Great job avoiding two soccer clues). Nice call out to Harold Ramis—Caddyshack? Groundhog Day? Ghostbusters? Who can forget his acting and directing. Lot of great clues today and misdirects—my favorites were MEZCAL, HELEN (Satan? Devil?) THOR? LINT? LOWGEAR? EPA? I could keep going. Like Sean I had ESCAPEART before ACTS and had to flyspeck, and BOOSTERTEAMS before SEATS until I got RAMIS. TICHA was a total no-know to me so that was no help. Also had to scratch my head to make sure I had HONSHU right as INHO was also an unknown. Did newer solvers solvers give up on this and say SCREWIT? I HOPE NOT, it was worth it. Last: again at the risk of angering the emus a few folks could not find my latest puzzle from Wednesday night on Crosshare. Again, SCREWIT, here’s the link if you need it: https://crosshare.org/crosswords/FISpD5Olay0ot2no6aw0/fur-better-or-fur-worse

Quick comment on the Wordplay column's reference to the old Minneapolis Lakers (which has nothing directly to do with the puzzle).

There are definitely still some who remember the Lakers as a local team.  They were the first NBA dynasty, winning multiple titles in the 40's and 50's.

When I moved to Minnesota in 1983, the team was of course long gone, but you would still occasionally see George Mikan, their greatest star, walking through the downtown skyways in Minneapolis.

Nothing to do with today's Crossword (which I greatly enjoyed, by the way), but a good memory.

Great puzzle. Many obfuscating and slippery clues. It did make me wonder where the word TELEPORT came from. It’s obviously a concocted hybrid of Greek “tele” (far) and Latin “port” (carry) but i wasn’t sure how far back it went, since obviously science fiction. A Google search pops up with an AI reading of Wikipedia, telling me that it was coined by American science fiction pioneer Charles Fort in 1931. Fort is a wonderful character whose occupation is given on Wikipedia as “Anomalistics researcher”. So, case closed. But hang on. Do we trust AI to give us the right answer? (Altogether now:) NO WE DON’T. So I delved into the Wikipedia page and its footnotes and — lo and behold — the term has been documented as far back as 1878. The wiki links to an issue of the Hawaiian gazette published on October 23, 1878. The Gazette has an article entitled “The Teleport.”, which in turn cites an unnamed Bombay paper that describes “an apparatus by which man can be reduced into infintisimal atoms, transmitted throngh a wire, and reproduced safe and sound at the other end.” It goes on to say how a dog was thus teleported, and a boy named Pedro, and then they were both teleported at the same time and their atoms got mixed up in an unfortunate accident. So a mysterious Bombay paper seems to have given us teleportation and the plot of “The Fly” all at once, almost 150 years ago! https://www.loc.gov/resource/sn83025121/1878-10-23/ed-1/?sp=4&st=text&r=0.588,0.773,0.125,0.175,0

EGIRLS was a new word for me, but now I know better. WE ARE SO BACK is definitely new and another term I probably won't ever use. Learning a new language is supposed to keep your brain young, but I'll stick to Beginners Italian (starting in October). Oh, and there's SCREAMO and MII. 

However, I did get quite of lot of this crossword, I am pleased to say, all the wordplay if not the names.

Oh, man, the spark in the box today!

Not just in the fresh answers (10 NYT debuts), but in the profusion of riddles in the clues, riddles that make you think, laugh, and maybe even exult.  Those riddles draw you in, get you involved, so much more than direct either-you-know-it-or-don’t clues.

The debut answers included BOOSTER SEATS, NON-ANSWER, WE’RE SO BACK, and WELL WELL WELL, which I can’t believe has never been in a Times puzzles before.

And those misdirecting wordplay riddles!   They lit up the solve, bringing me brain-ercize and sweet surprise.  Those that weren’t original were well chosen, and those that were, such as [Something read at a table] for TELL, [Screen capture?] for LINT, and [Organization that might do some spring cleaning?] for EPA – showed Jack’s clue-making prowess.

Jack, you’ve got the knack; please fast-track your way back.  Thank you for a stellar outing today!

While Pele is the Hawaiian goddess of the volcano, she did not create the islands. In Hawaiian mythology, the islands were pulled up from the bottom of the sea by Maui, with his fish hook, Mānaiakalani. Certain myths recognize the reality of volcanic activity, crediting Pele with both destroying the land (through eruptions) and expanding it.

For a moment, 
it feels like

WE ARE SO BACK.

NON-ANSWER is a wonderful clue/answer.  But I had to look at the finished puzzle to see how good it was since it wasn't in my own grid -- nor would it have been had I spent two entire days on trying to solve it.

It may be a little late in the day but I’d like to address this notion that puzzles should have only a certain number of proper nouns, as if that is some untouchable well of information am knowledge that is inaccessible to the common man. There are lots of non proper nouns that all people may not know—colloquial phrases, terms from specific specialties, outdated terms, etc. It would be a very unfortunate puzzle world where only words that “most” people know are in a grid, and we would learn nothing and hardly expand our horizons. 

The trick is to spread them out and try to cross terms that people from different walks of life may know. TRICHA, a WNBA player, crosses SAMANTHA a TV character and common name, and MII, a gaming term that is guessable and has been used before. RONALDINHO a soccer player, crosses HONSHU, a heavily populated important Japanese island that if you don’t know, you should be happy to learn. HAROLDRAMIS, an important director, crosses HELEN, a common name and one of the most important mythological characters. PELE crosses nothing obscure.

Is it hard? Sure, more to some than others. But it’s a PUZZLE. If, heaven forbid, there’s one or two letters you have to guess or leave ok up—or worse yet, you don’t get a gold star—why is that the end of the world? In every good puzzle there are words and names I don’t know, and can usually guess or figure out by crosses. That’s part of what makes it a good puzzle.

Just some idle thoughts on proper nouns:  Do the creators actually expect solvers to know obscure names?  Probably not.  (Not to offend anyone, but professional women's basketballers aren't exactly household names in America, let alone Poland and Japan.)

Half the fun of solving is the process of making known people and places you don't actually know.  It's fun to amaze yourself.

While I’m at it, I would also like to add that I feel very bent out of shape about EGIRLS being described as GenZ, having had girlfriends of mine try to be just that as early as the 2000s, as well as working with GenZ kids as an educator and can promise you that (at least the ones I work with) have no idea what they are. Regardless, this puzzle resurfaced some very old wounds for me regarding class difference. Things that I was always able to see, but never touch. Parties I would be asked to waitress, service, bartend for, but never be invited to. Grounds I knew deeply from every tree and branch and statue, with buildings on them containing worlds into which I’ll likely never go.
